title: Plain chance
goal: Learn to let Julia deal eight cards at random, over and over, and find how often 6 or more are springtails cards.
story: Itchy: "Start with a guess: what if each jar were a 50:50 coin toss?" This is practice. Toto deals eight cards, one for each practice jar, again and again, a fresh deal each time.
story_more: This is practice, made up for training. The practice notebook shows 6 of 8 jars with springtails. Toto asks: if each jar were a 50:50 coin toss, how often would 6 or more show springtails? He uses eight cards, one for each jar. He counts the springtails cards, deals eight new cards, and does it again, 1,000 times in all. The computer makes the cards, not real jars.

glossary.means: the words and symbols you type for Julia to follow.
the button that makes Julia follow your code and show the answer.
the button that puts the starting code back in the editor.
one row of code in the editor. Press Enter to start a new line.
say the answer you expect before you press Run. A wrong guess costs nothing.
several things in a row, between [ and ] with commas between them, such as [3, 8, 3].
one thing in a list.
the marks [ and ]. They go around a list.
the marks ( and ). The things a function works on go between them.
the mark , between one item and the next.
a word that does a job on what you give it. sum is a function.
one piece of information, such as the number 5 or the word true.
a word you give an answer, so later lines can use it. In n = 5, the name is n.
a special Julia word meaning yes. Write it in lower case. Here, a springtails card is true.
a special Julia word meaning no. Write it in lower case. Here, an empty card is false.
Julia's word for a value that is true or false. It starts with a capital B.
the marks " " around text. A number inside quotes is text, not a number.
letters and words, not numbers. In code, text goes inside quotes.
a number with no part after the point, such as 0, 1, 2 or 8.
the ___ in the editor. Replace it with your answer.
a check of two things that gives true or false, such as 5 >= 3.
means 'at least'. 5 >= 5 is true, and so is 6 >= 5.
this number or more. At least 5 means 5, 6, 7 and so on.
a dot before a comparison, as in .>=, asks every item in a list the same question.
a function that adds up a list. Each true counts as 1.
a function that counts the items in a list.
a function that deals things at random. rand(Bool, 8) deals eight values, each true or false.
share one number out by another. The slash / divides: 6 / 2 is 3.
one go of the card game: eight cards handed out at random, then the springtails cards counted.
how many. A deal's count is the number of springtails cards dealt.
a part out of the whole, found by dividing. 250 of 1,000 is a share of 0.25.
the list of Toto's 1,000 practice counts. 'Pretend' means made up by the computer.
the count in the practice notebook: 6 jars with springtails. 'Seen' means noticed.
the key that starts a new line of code.
the button that moves you on.
without looking at a worked line. Type what you remember.
the small mark . Put it before a sign such as >= to ask every item in a list.
a big letter, like the B in Bool.
one of the figures 0 to 9. Write 4, not the word four.
repeat the line once for each number after it. The _ is a name we never use.
decided by chance, with nobody choosing. The computer follows a rule that gives results that look random.

own_work.title: In your own work
own_work.say: You ran this above. In your work, change the 8 cards, the 6 and the 1:1000 deals. 1:1000 includes 1000, unlike Python's range(1000). _ is a name we never use. A binomial formula is a shortcut; dealing shows the idea.
own_work.code:
counts = [sum(rand(Bool, 8)) for _ in 1:1000]
events = counts .>= 6
sum(events) / length(events)

can_do: Make Julia deal random cards and count the springtails cards.
Compare all 1,000 counts at once with a dot.
Find how often a 50:50 guess matches a result, as a share.
close.common_mistake: Writing >= without the dot. Julia cannot compare a whole list with one number, unlike numpy and R.
